title: Why you hang on my plain words
english: I marvel at what has come over you when you hear my words, and how my voice has so overcome you. It comes from abroad and it is small, I suppose, with nothing to attract love, yet you seem to act toward me as iron acts toward a magnet. You hang from me, and each of you holds to one another, and all of you hold to God, from whom are all things and to whom are all things (Romans 11:36). What a wonderful chain, fitted together with unbreakable bonds, which the Holy Spirit weaves!

But the cause is not wisdom: as far as I know myself, I know nothing wiser than anyone else, unless someone counts this itself as my wisdom: to know that I am not wise, and not even near the true and first wisdom. The wise men of today fall far short of such judgment about themselves, since nothing is easier than to deceive oneself and, puffed up by empty pride, to think he is something when he is nothing (Galatians 6:3). Nor was I the first to preach to you the word of the orthodox faith, which you hold so firmly. I followed in the footsteps of others, and those footsteps are your own. The truth shall be told: you are disciples of Alexander, that excellent man, that great champion and herald of the Trinity, who drove out impiety by word and deed. For you remember that apostolic prayer which destroyed the author of impiety in a place that matched the filth of his tongue, so that insult might answer insult, and the unjust death of souls might be exposed to public shame by a just death.

So we broke open for you no strange spring, like the one Moses revealed in the dry land for those driven out of Egypt. We opened again a spring that lay hidden and choked up, like the servants of the great Isaac, who not only dug wells of living water but also cleared out those the Philistines had stopped up (Genesis 26:18-19). Nor am I one of the clever and charming speakers who steal goodwill by flattery. I see many among those who now promise to serve as priests who have turned our simple and artless devotion into something artful. They have carried a new kind of public maneuvering from the marketplace into holy things, and from the theaters into the worship hidden from the many. The result is two stages, if I dare say so. They differ as much as this: the one is open to all and the other to a few, the one is laughed at and the other is honored, the one is called theatrical and the other is called spiritual.

As Paul the Apostle says, “You are witnesses, and God,” that we do not belong to that party. We would sooner be accused of clumsiness and roughness than of fawning and servility. Even toward those most devoted to us we sometimes appear harsh in some place and at some moment, when they seem to act unreasonably toward us. This was shown by the recent innovation carried out upon me, when you the people, burning with zeal and anger, set me shouting and wailing upon this throne, which I do not know whether to call tyrannical or priestly. Set me you did, breaking the law through longing.
orientation: Gregory, newly installed in Constantinople, opens by marveling at the people's love for his preaching and denying that it comes from his own wisdom.

title: Why the people love him and his words
english: There I offended some of the hotter spirits so deeply that they broke away from me, turning their affection into hatred. I aim, you see, not so much at what will please people as at what will do them good.

What then is the reason for this great longing for me and for my preaching? Do you want to state and set it out yourselves, and explain your own feeling, or shall I publish it through my own lips, since you gladly use me to interpret so much else? I know you are giving the speech to me, as I judge from your silence. So listen, and judge whether I am a poor guesser at such things. First, I think, because you invited me yourselves, you are standing by your own judgment, and for that reason you cherish your own prey. It is human nature to look kindly on anything of our own, whether a possession or a child or an argument, and with willing favor to be won over by our own choices.

Second, you honor nothing in me so much as this, that I am not brazen or violent or theatrical and showy, but retiring and measured, almost a stranger in public life, solitary in manner, and, to put it most briefly, belonging to the philosophical life. And even that life I have not contrived with craft or calculation, but I honor it simply and spiritually. I do not hide myself to make people seek me, nor to seem worthy of greater honor, like those who show themselves for a moment and then withdraw. I do it to show by my quiet that I am fleeing the front seats and laying no claim to such honors.

Third, you see what I suffer from enemies attacking me outside and plotters scheming inside, since, as Daniel says, “Lawlessness came forth from elders in Babylon who seemed to judge Israel” (Susanna 5). You grieve and are indignant, and since you have no other way to help a man under tyranny, you offer the one gift that stands for all the rest, your pity. So pity mixed with respect has become affection. That is the secret of the honor you show me.

My preaching is the thing under attack, along with this fluent and envied tongue, which was trained in secular learning and which I have ennobled with divine truth. I have made bitter and undrinkable Marah sweet with the wood of life (Exodus 15:23), and you have felt something nobly generous in response. You love in me the very thing for which I am attacked. For why did I not embrace a mute and empty education? Why not one that is dry and drags downward? When I saw most people delighting in that, why did I utter strange and foreign wisdom and stand up against the opposing tongues? I should have run from argument with bold talk and called unreason faith, which I myself would have loved, as you well know, if I were a fisherman, since that is a ready excuse for ignorance among most people, if I had the power of miracles to serve in place of argument. May envy perish from among men, the extravagance of those who feel it and the poison of those who suffer it, the one passion that is both most unjust and most just: most unjust because it harasses everything good, most just because it consumes those who harbor it. I will not curse those who first praised me, for they did not know what their praises would lead to. If they had known, perhaps they would have added a little abuse to hold back envy.
orientation: Gregory is speaking to the people in Constantinople to explain the cause of their longing for him and his words as their support for their own choice, his retiring manner, and their pity for his suffering.

title: Envy through history and denial of seeking office
english: This same thing darkened the Morning Star, who fell through pride. Though he was divine, he could not bear not to be counted as God. This same thing drove Adam out of paradise, stealing him through pleasure and a woman. Kept for a time from the tree of knowledge, Adam was persuaded that he is begrudged being God. This same thing made Cain the murderer of his brother, for he could not bear a holier sacrifice. This same thing covered a disordered world with water and overwhelmed the people of Sodom with fire. This same thing buried Dathan and Abiram, who raged against Moses, and struck Miriam with leprosy, though she had only murmured against her brother. This same thing stained the earth with the blood of prophets and shook Solomon, the wisest of men, through women.

This same thing made Judas a traitor, stolen away for a little silver, a man worthy of the noose. This same thing made Herod a murderer of children and made Pilate a killer of Christ. This same thing winnowed Israel and scattered it, a sin from which its people have not risen even now. This same thing raised up against us the apostate tyrant, whose embers still pain us even now, though we have escaped the flame. This same thing cut apart the fair body of the church, dividing it into different and rival parties. This same thing has raised up against us our Jeroboam, the slave of sin, and lays a bond upon my tongue. For Jeroboam cannot bear the Trinity glorified, shining with the whole Godhead, and making her true heralds honored in your eyes. Do I seem to you to talk nonsense in drawing these parallels? Or has my written account rightly portrayed the causes of your love? On these matters, this is what I think.

Since I see some troubled by the insults against me, and making my dishonor into their own misfortune, come, let me reflect briefly on it in the spirit of the philosophical life. If I came to you with some petty human aim, laying claim to this see, and took authority over you with this gray hair and these limbs worn thin by time and sickness, or if I now bear this dishonor with such an aim, I would be ashamed before heaven and earth, by which even the ancients would swear. I would be ashamed before this see, and before this holy council, and before this holy and newly formed people, against whom so great a battle line of evil powers stands, to dissolve it before it holds together and to kill it before it is born, even as it is now being formed in Christ. I would be ashamed before my own toils and labors, before this threadbare clothing, and before the desert and the retreat where we lived together, before a life without comfort and a frugal table little better than the birds. Then let some speak the truth about me, that I desired another man's wife, though I refused to have a wife of my own. Then let even the Gibeonites have the advantage over me, whom I know the Holy Spirit does not admit even as woodcutters and water carriers, until they come to holy things with such stains on their life and speech. But if I came to plead for the faith, and to bring what help I could to the widowed and presently husbandless church, like caretakers and guardians who will give her in marriage to another, to one who proves worthy of her beauty and brings greater bridal gifts of virtue to the queen, then am I praiseworthy for my eagerness or blameworthy for what others suspect? For I am judged by passions that belong to others.
orientation: Gregory is speaking, continuing his catalogue of what envy does and then answering those embarrassed by the insults against him.

title: Seeming Is Nothing Beside Being
english: But, my good fellow, if we offer a hand to a ship tossed by a storm, or to a city under siege, or to a house being eaten by fire — bringing help with skiffs, or with a battle line, or with fire engines — you would still call us either those who sink ships, or lovers of that city or that house, and never its protectors and guardians.

"But most people do not see it that way," my opponent says. What difference does that make to me, for whom reason counts for more than being, or rather for everything? For reason is what condemned or acquitted me, what made me wretched or blessed. Seeming is nothing to me, like another person's dream. "You do not look that way to most people, fellow," he says. Does the earth stand still to the dizzy? To drunkards, do sober men look sober, and not walking on their heads or spinning around? Is honey not bitter to the sick and disordered when they taste it? Yet things are not so because sufferers think them so. Show me, then, that those who suppose this about me are healthy, and then advise me to change. Or condemn me, if I refuse persuasion and still stand by the same judgment. I do not look this way to most people, but I do to God. I do not merely look so; I stand revealed before him who knows all things before they come to be (Susanna 42), who fashions our hearts, each one alone, who understands all our works (Psalm 33:15), our stirrings and our thoughts, with which our deeds are done, from whom nothing that is escapes notice and nothing can escape, who sees our affairs differently than men see them. For man looks to the face, but God looks to the heart (1 Samuel 16:7). You have heard Scripture saying this, so believe it. He is the one anyone with sense must care for above all others together. If you took counsel from two men about the same matter, one wise and one ignorant, would you be thought sensible if you passed over the wiser and followed the more ignorant? Rehoboam won no praise for dishonoring the counsel of the elders and setting up the counsel of the young. When God and men are weighed against each other, will you prefer what men think? You will not, if you listen to me and think better.

"But we are ashamed of you because of your disgraces," he says. And I am ashamed of you, because you are ashamed. For if I suffer these things justly, I have more reason to be ashamed for myself than you have to be ashamed for me — not because I am dishonored, but because I deserve dishonor. If I suffer them unjustly, the charge belongs to those who insult me, and you should be indignant for them rather than for me; they are the ones in a bad way. If I were bad and you supposed me excellent, what should I have done? Become worse, to please you more? I would never have given myself that advice. So too, if you suppose me stumbling when I am doing right, I will not abandon doing right for your sake. For I live not more for you than for myself. I take reason as my counselor in everything, and the judgments of God, by which I am often convicted when no one accuses me, and acquitted when many condemn me. There is only one thing no one can escape: the court within and in ourselves. We must look to it alone and walk the straight road.
orientation: Gregory answers his opponents' objections that the many disapprove of him and that they are ashamed at the insults he suffers, as he denies desiring the see.

title: Staying the same and holding the confession
english: As for reputation, I will welcome it, to speak in human terms, when it comes. When it goes against me, I will let it go, and I will sacrifice nothing of being for the sake of seeming. For the matter stands like this. Whoever pursues what is good for the sake of something else has no firm hold on virtue. The moment that other thing passes, he stops pursuing the good. He is like a man who sails for profit and will sail no longer when there is no profit to be found. But whoever honors and cherishes the good for its own sake loves what stands firm, and so his zeal for it stands firm as well. He undergoes something divine, so that he can even speak the words of God, "But I am the same, and I have not changed" (Malachi 3:6).

So he will not be remade or shifted. He will not fall along with times and circumstances, becoming a different man at different moments and taking on many colors, like octopuses taking on the colors of the rocks they cling to. He will remain always the same, fixed among things that are not fixed and unturned among things that turn. He will be, I think, like a rock against the crash of winds and waves, unshaken itself and wearing down upon itself whatever strikes it. Enough of this, for I have no leisure to fight with tongues, and this is already perhaps more than is needed.

Now my words are for you, my flock. Paul says, "Become for me glory and joy and a crown of boasting" (1 Thessalonians 2:19). You are a defense before those who examine me. So just as builders or painters, when called to account, need only point to what they built or painted to be free of trouble, for, as the saying goes, a deed is stronger than a word, so I too shall rise above insults by pointing to you. And how shall I rise above them? First, if you guard unbent and firm your confession in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, adding nothing, removing nothing, and making nothing small in the one Godhead, for whatever is lessened is a lessening of the whole.

Send away those who think or say anything different, or who dissolve the unity by measuring it with natures or wall it apart, as a defilement of the church and a poison of the truth. Do this without hating them, but pitying their fall. Second, make your way of life follow right teaching, so that you embrace virtue fully and fall short in neither part.

You kings, revere the purple robe, for my sermon will legislate even for lawgivers. Know how great is what has been entrusted to you, and what is the great mystery concerning you. The whole world is under your hand, held by a small diadem and a short rag. What is above belongs to God alone, and what is below belongs also to you. Become gods to those beneath you, to say something even bolder. The heart of a king is in the hand of God (Proverbs 21:1), as has been said and is believed. Let your strength lie there, not in gold and armies. You who stand around the palace and the thrones, do not puff yourselves up too much on your offices, and do not think immortal thoughts about things that are not immortal. Remain faithful to the kings, and first to God, for whose sake you were entrusted to them and given over into their care. You who boast of your birth, ennoble your conduct, or I shall utter something unpleasant but noble. For only then would your birth be truly most noble, if the records did not also list the lowborn alongside you.
orientation: Gregory stops answering accusers and speaks to his own flock and then to emperors and courtiers about guarding the confession of the Trinity with a matching life.

title: Scolding the learned and the rich and the city to live well
english: You who are wise and learned, solemn in beard and worn cloak, you sophists and schoolmasters and hunters of public applause, I do not see how you can be called wise when you do not hold the first Word. You who cling to wealth, listen to the voice that says, "If wealth increases, do not set your heart on it" (Psalms 62:10). You know you are trusting something insecure.

Unload some cargo from your ship, so you may sail lighter. Perhaps you will snatch something from the enemy to whom all yours will pass. You who live for luxury, take something from your belly and give it to the spirit. The poor man is close at hand. Help his sickness. Belch forth into him some of your excess. Why should you labor with indigestion while he hungers? Why should you be drunk while he swells with dropsy? Why should you pile excess upon excess while he is wasted away by disease? Do not overlook your Lazarus here, or he will make you the rich man over there (Luke 16:19-31).

You, the great city, first straight after the first, or not even yielding that place, show yourselves first to me not in vice but in virtue, not in dissolution but in good order. It is shameful to rule cities yet be ruled by pleasures, to be restrained in everything else yet be so mad for horse races and theaters and stadiums and hunts that you make them your life, and the first of cities becomes a city of revelers, when it should be a fitting model of every good thing to all the rest.

May you spit out these things. May you become the city of God. May you be engraved on the hands of the Lord (Isaiah 49:16), and may you stand with us before the great founder of cities, radiant, in radiance at the last. This is the good news I bring you in Christ himself our Lord, to whom be glory, honor, and power forever. Amen.
orientation: Gregory closes by speaking in turn to the learned, the rich, lovers of luxury, and the great city itself to urge virtue.
